scenes.say: In 1943, Britain fooled Hitler with a dead man and a briefcase. And it helped change the course of World War Two.
The Allies were planning to invade Sicily. The problem was, it was the obvious target, and the Germans knew it.
So two British intelligence officers, Ewen Montagu and Charles Cholmondeley, came up with a very strange plan.
They would dress a dead body as a British officer, and let it wash up in Spain, chained to a briefcase of fake secret plans.
The body was Glyndwr Michael, a homeless Welshman who had died after swallowing rat poison. On paper, he became Major William Martin.
To make him believable, they filled his pockets with a fake life. Love letters from a fiancée, theatre tickets, even an unpaid bill.
scenes.sub: every detail had to be perfect

scenes.say: On April thirtieth, 1943, the submarine HMS Seraph slipped the body into the sea off Huelva, Spain.
scenes.sub: the body is released off Spain

scenes.say: Spain was neutral, but full of German agents. The secret letters were quietly copied, and passed on to Berlin.
The letters said the Allies would land in Greece and Sardinia. Germany believed them, and strengthened its defences there.
scenes.sub: Germany prepares for the wrong attack

scenes.say: Then, on July tenth, 1943, around one hundred and sixty thousand Allied troops landed on Sicily.
Historians call it one of the most successful deceptions of the entire war.
scenes.sub: one of the war's greatest deceptions

scenes.say: The lesson? The most convincing lie is the one people already expect. Germany feared an attack on Greece, so the fake plans felt true.
scenes.sub: we trust what we already expect

scenes.say: And Glyndwr Michael? He still lies in Huelva. Since 1998, his gravestone has carried his real name.
Follow Odd Archive for more true stories from history.
scenes.sub: for more true stories from history
